asr.full_text: Another question which is very applicable to you guys is, say I am a start-up and I'm pitching to you guys to raise money you've done this a long time in your experience what have been the traits I will ask each one of you individually traits in companies that have worked out and what have been the common traits in companies that haven't worked out? Give me two things that you have found in common between companies and founders that you've invested in that has worked out? There's usually the 180 of what works doesn't work. So one of them is my bias, as I said, for people who truly relate to the problem that they're solving, so which is aligned with what. And full ridden with potholes and shocks and emotional setbacks. The only thing that keeps you going is the mission. So if you have started with the purpose of saying, are there some quick bucks to be made here? I don't see it work. Okay, got it. So one thing you said is founders with long-term vision. Mission more than mission. Okay, vision, mission with something they relate with. Yes. A problem in their own personal lives. They want to solve for a long period of time. I think I'm back to over-indexing on one alpha female, alpha male, equivalent. Because I don't think you can distribute that vision and mission. Why one alpha male, one alpha female? No, meaning... Why not just one alpha male? That's what I meant. Either. I'm being gender neutral. One alpha male or one alpha male. So, I'm saying it's important for there to be one CEO, Uber founder CEO. And yes, theoretically, private equity or late stage growth can replace them saying these guys are useless. I'm trying to judge at seed, which is my bread and butter, whether they're capable of learning, inquisitive, and self-improving to become CEOs at every stage. Are those the top three traits you watch for? Inquisitive, curious curious and willing to learn? Yeah. Change in another word? Otherwise, no chance they can scale. You want to go next? No, I mean, see all the investments I've done in areas that I deeply care about- No, but how, in the investments you've done, what have you learned about them? No, that's why the only ones I think I associated with are, so I think, like Karthik said, I think you can be a CEO material, but you need a CTO in today's world, in whatever you're building. So it's also important, you know, when you meet, you want to see who's the guy who's going to help him. You know, if the person who's talking to you is the CEO, you need to see the quality of the CTO as well. You know, you can't- Big, big the CTO as well. You can't… I'm a big, big fan of co-founder. And, to Karthik's point, I mean, you need to be multiple, I mean, to make a company work, you need that right balance. In terms of personalities, you need these complementary skills. I want something interesting from Rajan. Toxic childhoods create great entrepreneurs. Something like that. Not the hardworking, obsessive, typical stuff. No, I mean, look, resilience, right? Look, on average, a successful startup will have several near-death moments. You run out of money, you get sued by a biggest competitor, your co-founder leaves. So I think being able to stick with it is really important. What has this founder, he or she or the founding team members, are there signs of resilience and just sticking with it and just going at it, right? And how do you discern that when you meet them? It depends on the experience, right? Like we ask the question, like, okay, actually they seed invested in this company called Ethereal Machines. No, I think you should write your values in ink and your strategy should change. But then if you do that, you can't be agile. No, agile— Basically, you know, I'm talking about the values. Your strategy should change. Values is what you're about, right? Like, you believe in x, and y, and so on. For example, what do you believe in? No, values of let's take… I'm a company. Should I even have values? Of course, you should. What are those? Focus on the— I take Google value that I love. So let's take, like you know, I'm a company, should I even have values? Of course, you should. What are those values? Focus on the like Google value that I love. Focus on the user and all else will follow. Do you think they really do that? Yeah. They focus on the user more than themselves? Yeah, focus on the user more than they focus on revenue, even today. Really? Absolutely. So, so going back, I think the first is resilience. Second is agility, meaning you meaning you're able to change. So, I think if you're going to be successful, 1 you're gonna have to go through many near-death moments and second you have to be able to change your strategy, change etc. – Change yourself? – You have to evolve, yeah. Actually, that would be the third thing, right? – When I said change your values and belief systems I asked whether the founder himself has to change what he thinks believes and lives. Many times- Constantly. About the market. I mean, if you separate out values of coin, and values, right? Like integrity is a value. You know what I mean? Like hopefully you're not changing that. Being customer obsessed is a value. Hopefully not changing that. You know, unless you're willing to go at it 10 to 15 years I think it's a thing where you've had some kind of pressure and no one really thinks that, you have so much value. So, you've put yourself under pressure. And then you finally realize that you are not changing your own value. And that's an extremely good thing. So, you really have to be willing to go ahead and take a step or two to change the value, hopefully you're not changing that. Unless you're willing to go ahead at 10 to 15 years... making very little money, going through really excruciating times, have five days a week and all of that, but... Like, you know, so it... I lived in my office for six years. No, that's my point. Right? That's my point. Exactly. There you go. My bedroom was in the cabin. I thought you were questioning. I'm like, okay. You guys are talking about five days a week, nine to five, and fields are over. No, but I'll tell you where the dichotomy arrives in this conversation. I feel hard work in the mainstream is a way of appeasing our ego, both as a consolation and as a reward. Consolation, when things don't work out, I can tell myself, but I worked hard. When I win, appeasing my ego on the other end, because everyone can argue, like probably the watchman of my apartment works three times as hard as me. So can you really correlate hard work to success? Absolutely. Necessary, but not sufficient. I go back to that argument. I don't, it's not a guarantee! But like that everything is necessary. I'll tell you why. No, I agree with you there. Hard work is a precondition. It is. But it is not the main condition. You might have gotten lucky by getting enough capital to be able to buy some of that on the cheap, in a hot market, etc. But actually, the more capital you get, if you're a responsible entrepreneur, your work just increased again, right? So it's never-ending in my view. Because your organization does not hit steady state. Neither does your customer base, neither does your product. Any time in the near future. Yeah, but Kartik, see, the thing here is, I am looking for nuance. If people watching this are told, you need to be hard-working, you need to do this, what are they learning from us? No, this is not hard working. Hard working is not 7 days a week, 18 hours, 15 hours a week. Okay, you need to be obsessively hardworking. This is insanely hard-working. You know the generic, right? I know. But the thing is, as you know more than anybody else, this is not rocket science. This guy, just as an example, Ethereal. He asked me last week when I'm in Bainglore and he has hacked a meeting with me at the airport tomorrow to get that extra hour . So you want evidence? That's the kind of evidence. Is it networking skill in today's world to be able to have gotten that meeting with you either through a referral or something? No, this is my profounder for five years. No, but is that a very important thing? Absolutely. Those are the kind of things I want. I've had Narayan Murthy's car door to ask him for money. Yeah, give me that then. No, that's what I'm saying. No, but you have to push. And that's not me, by the way. I had to play out the scene in my head on how I would interrupt him on his walk from the podium, to his car, ten times. And then the last chance was the door was shutting, so I had to hold it. That's not me. Okay, you give me one now. Storyteller. Yeah. So Can you really tell the story in a way that's interesting? Very few founders can. If somebody is looking to build product ahead of insight, and a deeper appreciation for what really the problem is, I think I've seen that as a recipe for disaster in most companies. What they will have is 100 member-member tech team, no right, average product, very average product because they have not gotten enough insight so I think this thing that you need good tech is a hardworking is a prerequisite but how you apply it, how the hard work you can direct your hard work. So that's what I wanted to kind of, even the a hard work, you can direct your hard work. So that's what I wanted to kind of, even in the hard work discussion, you can direct it with the right hustle in the right way to achieve a right end goal, right? Or it can be just misdirected, feel good hard work. Actually, I won. So I think outside all of this, it's just people skills. You know, just to be able to keep your team together. I think what he's trying to say is psychologically, even as alpha male you need to be more accepting of your feminine side. From a very psychological standpoint. It's more than that, I think... That's what I said, you've got to become a coach. There are no boundaries there. Because that societal construct, screwed up childhoods, staying away from privileged upbringing is something to look for. Like, you know? Staying away, I don't know. But you know, I think I'm the first to admit. You could look for it, by the way. But as a founder, you know, the question is you can, I mean, if you did have a screwed up… You can't reverse your life. You can't chase that, right? You could have a privileged background but if you're not willing to work seven days a week… I'm asking you, what you look for. No, no. Don't drown that emotion. Have you ever met someone who has told you and truly believed that they love their childhood? No. A lot of people. No, you're right! They're extracting something for a right to win. And they're saying, this is my proof to the world that I can win. And they're extracting some part of course, they'll be extracting most of it. I think I'd also say that trying to tell a story that's not real very quickly because this is what we do for a living. We meet thousands of founders. Another thing I was hoping somebody would say, authenticity. Say it like it is. Yeah. Authenticity to the extent. You have no automation in the business, say it like it is. I got 500 people packing stuff. Okay, great. At least you told me that. Authenticity to the extent of self-recognition where you are not pretending to be a machine. You are not pretending to be a saint, you are not pretending to be anything, but you are cognizant to the fact that you are greedy, you are jealous, you are insecure, like every one of us sitting here is. So the time spent pretending to be a person that does not have those traits is futile. And if somebody recognises that, I think it's extremely appealing and endearing. So this whole idea of founder market fit, as much as important as product market fit is, in 10 years, will you love doing it? You're passionate about the space, but the space requires execution, the space requires you to solve a problem and that typically requires different skills and characteristics that may not be natural to you and are you willing to change? And are you willing to become that different person? You know, like, I mean I was talking about these B2B manufacuton startups. I'm seeing these founders struggling because they all thought this is entrepreneurship and startups meant tech. And now they're figuring out these are really heavy lifting problems. Stay true to the mission. So my question was really, one, you're going through tough times. And then one, you're going through tough times, right? And then one, you're going through good times. Tough times, you kind of know, people, if a business breaks, it's a tough time when it broke. But are there many times where companies are going through good times and they break because co-founders don't get along well? Happens. Happens. You know, they start out with the same kind of passion, you know, focus and the business takes a different shape. It's doing well, but it's become a different business. And one of them relates to that different business. And the other one does not relate to it. It's also sometimes it could be that the CEO persona has evolved to something and the No. 2 and No. 3 in hierarchy, for what it is worth, is not as motivated to continue doing the same thing or it has become less relevant.
